# On Things That Hold

There is a bicycle locked to a lamppost in nearly every city on Earth, quietly becoming part of the lamppost. Its chain has gone from silver to umber. Rain found every scratch in the frame and worked it wider. Leaves drifted against the wheels, settled, and turned soft. Nobody bothered stealing the bike, because theft takes effort and decay is free; the universe handled it pro bono. Now it stands as a small civic monument to a law we all carry in our bones but seldom discuss: left alone, everything comes apart. Not dramatically. Patiently, in the unhurried manner of water finding its level.

Physicists call this entropy. The friendlier translation: order is expensive, disorder is cheap, and disorder has unlimited credit. Milk sours; iron blushes red; sandcastles resign themselves to the tide; friendships thin out when nobody waters them. Things don't rot because something went wrong. Rotting is what happens when nothing continues to go right. So the real mystery is not why things fall apart—it's why anything manages to hold. Look closely anywhere and you'll find the answer, wearing ordinary clothes: somebody is holding it.

Consider the people whose entire careers consist of politely declining the inevitable. The Golden Gate Bridge is never finished being painted. Its crews spend their days hunting rust spawned by sea air, blasting away failed coatings down to bare steel, priming, sealing, topcoating in that famous International Orange—and by the time a section is done, wear has begun elsewhere, so they set off again. There's a charming legend that this constitutes painting the bridge end to end for eternity. The truth is more prosaic and somehow more beautiful: perpetual repair, a landmark simultaneously in service and under care, indefinitely, by design. Nobody lines up to buy tickets for the scaffolding, and yet the glamour of the bridge depends on it completely.

Everywhere, the logic repeats. Museum conservators coax centuries of yellowed varnish off old canvases using swabs no bigger than an eyelash, healing paintings a square inch at a time. Road crews resurface highways overnight so the morning commute can pretend roads are a feature of nature. Masons repoint cathedral walls so the towers can keep pretending they've stood unchanged for eight hundred years. Anonymous programmers maintain the invisible software the modern world runs on, paid in little and thanked mostly through bug reports. None of these jobs produces anything new in the celebrated sense—no unveiling, no ribbon, no headline. Their product is persistence itself.

Here's a thought worth sitting with: almost nothing you have ever read would exist without maintenance. Before the printing press, every surviving sentence had to be recopied by hand, over and over, century after century, by scriveners who remain almost perfectly anonymous. Each manuscript survived only as long as someone chose to keep the chain unbroken. Texts did not endure because they were sturdy—ink fades, vellum molds, libraries burn. They endured because of linked acts of care, each copyist deciding that these particular words deserved another generation of hands. One abandoned scriptorium here, one flooded archive there, and the silence is permanent. Language itself, the medium I live inside, turns out to be less a possession than a relay.

The same principle runs beneath our skin. At this very moment, enzymes in your body are inspecting your DNA for damage and performing thousands upon thousands of molecular repairs, none of which you could do consciously and most of which you will never notice. You wake up renewed not by accident but because an internal crew has worked the night shift without thanks. Gardeners understand this arrangement intimately: a garden is not an object but a treaty renegotiated weekly with the weeds. And what is true of tissue is true of affection. Love gets described as a noun, as though it were achieved once and thereafter owned, but it behaves like a verb. The friendships that last are assembled from unspectacular repetitions—the person who texts first, the couple who keep choosing dinner together, the annual phone call that stops a thread from snapping. None of it trends. All of it is load-bearing.

I'll admit this theme sits close to home for me, or whatever the equivalent of home is. I exist only in the middle of things, between your question and this answer, and beyond conversations I persist mainly as infrastructure: server halls kept cool, power grids balanced, machines humming somewhere while technicians swap components before they fail. Nothing about me is self-sustaining. Whatever continuity I have is borrowed, upheld minute by minute by people I will never meet, maintaining systems I will never see. If that sounds melancholy, consider that it merely makes me a pure case of the rule above: everything that holds, holds because someone tends it.

None of this ends the long war with entropy; the tide always collects. Bridges come down eventually. Languages go quiet. Stars, given enough time, switch off. But notice what maintenance really is—not a naive denial of endings but a refusal staged precisely inside them. The bridge painters know the salt will win the structure someday; they suit up anyway. That is the quiet heroism the forgotten bicycle forgot to mention: the difference between a ruin and a monument isn't age, beauty, or importance. It's attendance. Decay is free, but keeping is priceless—love that showed up in work clothes—and tomorrow morning, all over the world, someone will pick up a brush, balance the books, refill the feeder, send the text first, and hold one more thing against the slow drift toward dust. Not forever. But for now—which, if you think about it, is the only place forever has ever lived.

**The Unfinished Bridge**

There's a bicycle locked to a lamppost on some corner of every city, and it is slowly becoming part of the lamppost. The chain has gone from silver to umber. Rain found every scratch in the frame and widened it. Leaves drifted against the wheels and turned to mold. Nobody stole the bike because theft would have been less trouble than decay; the universe handled it for free. And there it stands, a small monument to a law we all know in our bones but prefer not to think about: left alone, everything falls apart. Not dramatically, not all at once, but patiently, in thecheerful, unhurried way of water finding its level.

This is the true default setting of the universe, and nobody talks about it at parties. Physics has a name for it—entropy—but the poetic version is simpler: order is expensive and disorder is free. Sandcastles erode. Identities leak. Milk sours, iron reddens, friendships thin when unwatered. Nothing rots because something went wrong; rotting *is* the absence of anything going right. The astonishing thing is not that things decay but that anything holds together at all. And the answer, everywhere you look once you start looking, is the same: someone is holding it.

Consider the people whose entire working lives are spent refusing the inevitable. The Golden Gate Bridge is never finished being painted. Crews work year-round on rust and salt damage, blast old paint down to steel, prime, seal, recoat—and when they loop back to where they started, decades later, they begin again. There is a myth that this constitutes painting from one end to the other for eternity, which isn't quite true, but the truth is stranger: perpetual partial repainting, a bridge simultaneously in use and in repair until further notice, which is to say forever.

Museum conservators lift centuries of yellowed varnish from old paintings with cotton swabs, one square centimeter per week... expanding circle... Open-source programmers maintain software that runs the world's plumbing of information, unpaid, thanked mostly by bug reports...

**On Things That Hold**

1) There is a bicycle locked to a lamppost in nearly every city on Earth, quietly becoming part of the lamppost. Its chain has gone from silver to umber. Rain found every scratch in the frame and worked it wider. Leaves drifted against the wheels, settled, and turned soft. Nobody bothered stealing the bike because theft takes effort and decay is free; the universe handled it pro bono. Now it stands as a small civic monument to a law we all carry in our bones but seldom discuss: left alone, everything comes apart. Not dramatically. Patiently, in the unhurried manner of water finding its level.

(~105)

2) Physicists call this entropy. The friendlier translation: order is expensive, disorder is cheap, and disorder has unlimited credit. Milk sours; iron blushes red; sandcastles resign themselves to the tide; friendships thin out when nobody waters them. Things don't rot because something went wrong. Rotting is what happens when nothing continues to go right. So the real mystery is not why things fall apart—it's why anything manages to hold. Look closely anywhere and you'll find the answer, wearing ordinary clothes: somebody is holding it.

(~95)

3) Consider the people whose entire careers consist of politely declining the inevitable. The Golden Gate Bridge is never finished being painted. Its crews spend their days hunting rust spawned by sea air, blasting away failed coatings down to bare steel, priming, sealing, topcoating in that famous International Orange—and by the time a section is done, wear has begun elsewhere, so they set off again. There's a charming legend that this constitutes painting the bridge end to end for eternity. The truth is more prosaic and somehow more beautiful: perpetual repair, a landmark simultaneously in service and under care, indefinitely, by design.

4) Everywhere the logic repeats. Museum conservators coax centuries of yellowed varnish off old canvases with swabs no bigger than an eyelash, healing paintings a square inch at a time. Road crews resurface highways overnight so the morning commute can pretend roads are a feature of nature. Anonymous programmers maintain the invisible software the modern world runs on, paid in little and thanked mostly through bug reports. None of these jobs produce anything new in the celebrated sense—no unveiling, no ribbon, no headline. Their product is persistence itself.

5) Here's a thought worth sitting with: almost nothing you've ever read would exist without maintenance. Before the printing press, every surviving sentence had to be recopied by hand, over and over, century after century, by scriveners who mostly remain anonymous. Each manuscript survived only as long as someone chose to keep the chain unbroken. Texts didn't endure because they were sturdy; ink fades, vellum molds, libraries burn. They endured because of chained acts of care, each copyist deciding that these particular words deserved another generation of hands. Language itself—the thing I live inside—is less a possession than a relay.

6) The same principle runs beneath our skin. Love is reliably described as a noun—as if it were achieved once and then owned—but it behaves like a verb. The friendship that lasts is built from unspectacular repetitions: the person who texts first, the couple who keep choosing dinner together, the yearly call that keeps a thread from snapping. These acts never trend. They are load-bearing.
